title: Legal Trios: Reflecting on the Legal Profession with Prof. David Wilkins at Annual Meeting
author: Jonathan Schreiber

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source identifies faster information technology, blurred boundaries between law and business, and potentially durable structural change, but it does not address buyer-led workflow unbundling, time-based pricing, task allocation, junior training or verification. Its broad account is compatible with the cluster but insufficient to show acceptance or rejection of its principal proposition.

st.t: Lawyer development: AI renews lifelong competence reform
st.an: Wilkins accepts the need to modernize lawyer development beyond technical legal competence and materially extends the proposition by linking training to interdisciplinary judgment, institutional redesign, inclusion, access to justice and collective systemic reform. He is cautious about declaring a definitive paradigm shift and does not specifically develop AI verification or curricular-effectiveness evidence.
qs: He highlighted two main points to consider:  - Law is a human capital profession, done by people for people, even if those people work for huge corporations, so lawyers need to think about how they recruit, train, develop, and relate to people.

The only way we can preserve the core principles of the legal profession and excellence in practice, while at the same time advancing to become more diverse and provide more service to broader constituencies is by coming together to effectuate systemic change.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Wilkins supports the need for technology-enabled work and service redesign, then materially broadens it into profession-wide institutional reform. He adds concrete emphasis on paraprofessionals, self-help resources, cross-boundary collaboration and new approaches to developing legal skills, although he does not address AI’s jagged capabilities or verification requirements directly.
qs: This includes increasing the use of technology, expanding the role for paraprofessionals, and investing in more resources for self-help.

The only way we can preserve the core principles of the legal profession and excellence in practice, while at the same time advancing to become more diverse and provide more service to broader constituencies is by coming together to effectuate systemic change.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s broad conclusion that technology and other systemic forces are restructuring, rather than eliminating, the legal profession. His emphasis on recruitment, training and development aligns with concern for the profession’s human-capital pipeline, while his claim that demand for lawyers is increasing weighs against wholesale displacement. However, the source does not specifically assess generative AI, junior-task automation or current employment evidence.
qs: He highlighted two main points to consider:  - Law is a human capital profession, done by people for people, even if those people work for huge corporations, so lawyers need to think about how they recruit, train, develop, and relate to people.
- The need for lawyers today is greater than ever because of globalization and the increasing complexity of the world.

kp.k: Post-2008 disruption may represent lasting structural change
kp.d: Reporting David Wilkins’s 2016 keynote, the article says that pessimism about Big Law and lawyers since 2008 coincided with under-resourced courts, budget-constrained agencies, unmet legal need, and worsening law-school enrollment and employment outcomes. Wilkins treats the permanence of these developments as uncertain, while suggesting that the financial crisis accelerated changes already developing gradually.
qs: Since 2008, the outlook has been less than optimistic, with scholars talking about “the death of Big Law” and “the end of lawyers.”
So the question, Wilkins explained is, are these problems part of a paradigm shift or simply a temporary correction that will soon re-adjust?

It’s too early to tell for sure, but it seems likely that a lot of these changes are here to stay and may have been coming more gradually anyway, but were simply pushed into high gear by the recent financial crisis.

kp.k: Technology is one of three profession-shaping developments
kp.d: Wilkins identifies increasingly fast and sophisticated information technology alongside economic globalization and the erosion of traditional knowledge boundaries as broad developments affecting law and other professions. The source does not discuss particular AI systems, legal tasks, adoption evidence, or measured effects.
qs: These changes are not unique to the legal profession, either.
A rise in the speed and sophistication of information technology.
The blurring together of traditional knowledge, whereby things that used to be considered separate and distinct are now inextricably linked.

kp.k: Law reacts slowly to technological and social change
kp.d: Wilkins characterizes law as a lagging indicator because of its reliance on history and precedent. His argument implies an institutional adaptation problem: the profession may recognize external changes late and respond even later, although the article supplies no empirical measurement of this lag.
qs: The law is a lagging, not a leading indicator of change, which is unsurprising given its focus on history and precedent.
Unfortunately, that can also make it slow to recognize change, and even slower to react to it.

kp.k: Legal work is becoming increasingly institutionalized
kp.d: Wilkins says legal practice is shifting away from predominantly solo and small-firm settings toward larger law firms and expanding public legal offices. He calls this an “institutionalized profession” and argues that ethical rules and practice arrangements remain oriented toward older settings; the source does not identify particular rules or quantify the shift.
qs: Practice is shifting from mostly solo and small firm practice to large law firms.
At the same time, the size of public legal offices such as attorneys general is growing, as is the number of attorneys employed by the courts.
In short, the law is becoming an “institutionalized profession.”
However, the ethical rules and other aspects of practice are still geared towards the historic practice settings and styles.

kp.k: Legal practice increasingly intersects with business and nonlawyers
kp.d: The article presents the boundary between law and business as an example of formerly distinct knowledge domains becoming interconnected. It also reports growing global diversity and a greater need for lawyers to interact with nonlawyers, supporting Wilkins’s broader argument that contemporary lawyers must understand law’s intersection with other issues.
qs: He highlighted a few examples, such as public and private spheres, global and local impacts, and more relevantly, law and business.
Furthermore, global diversity continues to increase, as well as the need for interaction with non-lawyers.
However, this also requires lawyers to understand the intersection of law and other issues.

kp.k: Competition extends beyond firms to future legal talent
kp.d: Wilkins describes intense competition among lawyers and firms and for high-achieving students considering different professions. His recommendation is to preserve professional integrity and service-oriented careers while modernizing legal practice so that law can continue attracting talented entrants.
qs: Competition is intense, not only amongst lawyers and firms, but also in the pipeline of smart students to become future lawyers.

Wilkins discussed the need for retaining the core integrity of the profession in order to continue to attract talented people who want challenging and rewarding service careers, while also considering changes to modernize practice and compete with other fields attracting top students.

kp.k: Law remains fundamentally a human-capital profession
kp.d: Wilkins argues that legal services remain work performed by people for people, including when clients are large corporations. He therefore emphasizes recruitment, training, development, and professional relationships as central concerns rather than treating technological or organizational change as eliminating the human dimension of legal work.
qs: Law is a human capital profession, done by people for people, even if those people work for huge corporations, so lawyers need to think about how they recruit, train, develop, and relate to people.

kp.k: Complexity increases demand for cross-disciplinary lawyers
kp.d: Wilkins claims that globalization and growing world complexity make lawyers more necessary, not less. This is a qualitative argument rather than a measured finding, and it is conditioned on lawyers gaining an understanding of legal issues’ connections with other domains.
qs: The need for lawyers today is greater than ever because of globalization and the increasing complexity of the world.
However, this also requires lawyers to understand the intersection of law and other issues.

kp.k: Technology and paraprofessionals could expand access to justice
kp.d: Wilkins attributes unmet legal need partly to the expense of training and developing lawyers, which makes legal services unaffordable for many. He recommends more efficient methods of developing legal skills and delivering services, specifically including technology, broader paraprofessional roles, and greater self-help resources. The article offers no implementation model or outcome evidence.
qs: There are not enough lawyers to serve all of those in need, largely because the expense of training and developing lawyers prices many out of being able to afford legal services.
Therefore, we need to be open to new ways to more efficiently develop legal skills and provide legal services.
This includes increasing the use of technology, expanding the role for paraprofessionals, and investing in more resources for self-help.

kp.k: Inclusion requires institutions themselves to change
kp.d: On access to the legal profession, Wilkins argues that increased diversity requires more than asking individuals to conform to existing institutions. He recommends changing institutional structures and foundational assumptions that prevent talent from being fully used.
qs: We need to increase diversity and strive for true inclusion by shifting our perception that individuals need to change to fit within existing institutions to changing the institutions themselves and the assumptions at their core that inhibit maximization of talent.

kp.k: Lawyers need technical, counselling, and leadership capabilities
kp.d: Wilkins describes three roles for lawyers: astute technicians, wise counsel, and leaders. He regards technical legal competence as an existing strength, while presenting moral judgment and change leadership as more challenging capabilities requiring lawyers to move beyond narrow advisory work.
qs: Wilkins provided another trio – the three roles lawyers need to play:
Astute technicians – Lawyers already do a good job of this – being competent in the law and understanding complex issues.
Wise Counsel – This one is often more challenging, requiring lawyers to combine principles of law and morality.
Leaders – This one also presents challenges, whereby lawyers have to go beyond being merely advisors but to also be the agents of change they want to see.

kp.k: Systemic adaptation requires collaboration across professional boundaries
kp.d: Wilkins urges lawyers to work collectively and across boundaries involving legal practice, legal education, and nonlawyers. He frames coordinated systemic change as necessary to preserve professional principles and excellence while improving diversity and extending service to broader constituencies.
qs: They need to reach across boundaries, not only within the legal profession, but also beyond to legal education and non-lawyers.
Wilkins ended with a plea for lawyers to work together.

The only way we can preserve the core principles of the legal profession and excellence in practice, while at the same time advancing to become more diverse and provide more service to broader constituencies is by coming together to effectuate systemic change.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no AI-specific claims. Its closest relevant claim is Wilkins’s recommendation to increase technology use, alongside paraprofessionals and self-help resources, to address unmet legal need.
pts.d: Jonathan Schreiber’s account attributes this recommendation to Professor David Wilkins. Technology is discussed generically, not as artificial intelligence. Wilkins links unaffordable legal services to the expense of training and developing lawyers and calls for more efficient ways to develop legal skills and deliver services. This is a proposed direction for reform, not a demonstrated technology outcome or a prediction of AI-driven substitution.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The technology recommendation rests on Wilkins’s expert analysis; no empirical evidence of technology’s effects is supplied.
pts.d: The article identifies Wilkins’s legal-profession research credentials and reports his keynote remarks. It provides no data, benchmarks, named technology deployments, or measured efficiency or access-to-justice improvements supporting this recommendation. Links concerning unmet legal need provide background, but the supplied text does not report findings from them that establish technology’s effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The recommendation is forward-looking from October 2016, with no adoption deadline or quantified forecast.
pts.d: Technology use is presented as part of a future access-to-justice reform agenda, in response to existing affordability barriers. The source does not specify a particular technology, implementation timetable, or conditions under which technology would achieve a measurable improvement. It places technology alongside other reforms rather than presenting it as a standalone solution.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The intended beneficiaries are people unable to afford legal services; the proposed changes also concern lawyers, paraprofessionals, and people using self-help resources.
pts.d: Wilkins’s recommendation addresses unmet legal need rather than enterprise legal-cost savings. It envisages more efficient legal-skill development and service provision, a larger role for paraprofessionals, and more self-help resources. The account does not identify AI-specific effects on law-firm staffing, lawyer employment, particular practice areas, or provider market shares.
